narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being ranked in the second decile in Year 3 is well below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted, signaling weaker academic performance in the later stages of your studies. This was the single biggest reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your family income bracket came next. Being from a middle-income family actually worked slightly in your favor compared with the accepted group, where upper-middle and high-income backgrounds are more common. This factor mildly pulled the prediction back toward passing.

Your undergraduate GPA ranked third. At 2.5 it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore nudged the outcome slightly toward failure, though its effect was smaller than your third-year class rank.

Taken together, the model saw your lower academic standing in later law school years and modest undergraduate grades as outweighing the modest positive signal from your family background. 

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, enrolling in a structured bar-prep program, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying. Improving those academic signals will be the most direct way to change future predictions in your favor. (248 words)
